facts.statement: Ultrastenos was a small crocodilian measuring upwards of 1.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: Ultrastenos was a small mekosuchine, measuring upwards of 1.5 m long.

facts.statement: The genus Ultrastenos was described in 2016 based on a holotype specimen found at the Low Lion Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area.
facts.quote: The genus Ultrastenos, meanwhile, was described almost 20 years later in 2016 based on the holotype specimen QM F42665, a posterior cranium and mandible found at the Low Lion Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area.

facts.statement: The type species of Ultrastenos was originally designated as Ultrastenos willisi.
facts.quote: type_species: Ultrastenos willisi

facts.statement: The species Ultrastenos huberi was originally described as a subdivision of the genus.
facts.quote: subdivision: U. huberi (Willis, 1997)

facts.statement: It is debated whether Ultrastenos had a slender snout; later studies suggest the initial interpretation of a narrow mandible was a misinterpretation and the animal actually had a more generalized lower jaw.
facts.quote: However, a later study found that this was a misinterpretation of the fossil specimen and that Ultrastenos instead had a more generalized lower jaw.

facts.statement: Research suggests that the fossils of Ultrastenos and the previously named species Baru huberi belong to the same animal.
facts.quote: The same publication also provided evidence that the fossils of Ultrastenos belonged to the same animal previously named "Baru" huberi

facts.statement: It is debated whether certain cranial fossils belong to Ultrastenos or to the species Baru wickeni, with some researchers proposing they belong to a juvenile Baru wickeni.
facts.quote: Yates' paper on Baru further questioned the referral of one of the White Hunter crania (QM F31075) to Ultrastenos, instead proposing that it belonged to a juvenile Baru wickeni

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that a re-description of the taxon was necessary following the discovery of related forms.
facts.quote: The team, which included Stein, alluded to a re-description of the taxon being in the works following the discovery of a related form.

facts.statement: Due to priority rules, the valid species name is Ultrastenos huberi, honoring Professor Huber.
facts.quote: Consequently, this created the combination Ultrastenos huberi, with the species name honoring Professor Huber, who was employed as rector at the University of Bonn, Germany.

facts.statement: Ultrastenos had a flattened and short snout, contrary to earlier proposals that it was elongated.
facts.quote: Ultrastenos, contrary to its name, had a snout described as platyrostral and brevirostrine skull, meaning its snout was flattened and short rather than elongated as initially proposed by Stein and colleagues

facts.statement: The external nostrils of Ultrastenos were positioned very close to the tip of its snout, giving the premaxilla a steep profile.
facts.quote: The external nares are positioned rather closely to the very tip of the snout, which makes the premaxilla appear steep when seen in profile view

facts.statement: The nostrils of Ultrastenos were longer than wide and opened slightly forward rather than straight up, unlike many semi-aquatic crocodilians.
facts.quote: Overall the naris is longer than it is wide and directed anterodorsally, meaning it opens slightly towards the front of the skull rather than facing purely upwards as is typically seen in many semi-aquatic crocodilians

facts.statement: The nasal bones of Ultrastenos extended across the snout and touched the nostrils.
facts.quote: The nasal bones stretch across the rostrum and come into contact with the nares

facts.statement: The supratemporal openings in the skull of Ultrastenos were prominent and teardrop-shaped.
facts.quote: The supratemporal fenestrae are prominent and teardrop-shaped, as noted by both Stein and colleagues in 2016 and Yates and Stein in 2024

facts.statement: Adult Ultrastenos possessed four premaxillary teeth according to Yates and Stein.
facts.quote: Yates and Stein describe Ultrastenos as having had four premaxillary teeth in adults

facts.statement: The number of maxillary teeth in Ultrastenos is uncertain but likely ranged between 14 and 15 on each side.
facts.quote: The precise number of maxillary teeth is uncertain, but was likely somewhere between 14 and 15 teeth on either side

facts.statement: Most maxillary teeth of Ultrastenos were subcircular and lacked significant side-to-side compression.
facts.quote: Overall most teeth of the maxilla are described as subcircular, meaning that they lacked significant labiolingual compression

facts.statement: The exact number of lower jaw teeth in Ultrastenos is unknown, though Yates and Stein suggest a minimum of 16.
facts.quote: The precise tooth count of the lower jaw is unknown, but Yates and Stein suggest a minimum of 16 mandibular teeth based on the various fossils that have been collected

facts.statement: The tibia of Ultrastenos differed from modern crocodiles by being flattened front-to-back and having a shaft that became more square further from the hip.
facts.quote: The only difference between the tibia of Ultrastenos and modern crocodiles is that in the mekosuchine it is flattened front to back and the shaft becomes more square as it moves away from the hip

facts.statement: Willis previously considered Ultrastenos and Baru to be the same genus, using skull features to distinguish between them.
facts.quote: Willis compared this condition to Baru wickeni and used it to differentiate Ultrastenos from Baru darrowi when he still considered these animals to be congeneric

facts.statement: There is a disagreement regarding the number of premaxillary teeth in juvenile Ultrastenos, with older claims of five teeth based on a specimen now classified as Baru wickeni contrasting with newer findings.
facts.quote: Yates and Stein describe Ultrastenos as having had four premaxillary teeth in adults, stating that the number seen in hatchlings is not known. This contrasts with Willis' older claim that juveniles had five premaxillary teeth, which was based on a specimen now referred to Baru wickeni

facts.statement: The holotype skull of the species previously known as Baru huberi measures approximately 20 cm in length and 11 cm in width.
facts.quote: The holotype skull of "B." huberi measures approximately 20 cm long with a width of around 11 cm

facts.statement: Stephen Wroe estimated the total body length of the animal previously known as Baru huberi to be around 1.5 meters.
facts.quote: Stephen Wroe estimating a total length of around 1.5 m for the animal

facts.statement: The fossil material used to establish the genus Ultrastenos in 2016 measured 16 to 18 cm wide between the quadrates and approximately 35 cm in length.
facts.quote: The material used to establish Ultrastenos in 2016 was however significantly larger, measuring 16-18 cm wide between the quadrates and some 35 cm in length

facts.statement: Stein and colleagues initially proposed that Ultrastenos was a longirostrine animal with jaws long and narrow like modern gharials.
facts.quote: Initially, Stein and colleagues proposed that Ultrastenos could have been a longirostrine animal, meaning that unlike in any other known mekosuchine, the jaws would have been long and narrow like in modern gharials

facts.statement: The teeth in the mandible of Ultrastenos are molariforms, which contradicts the needle-like caniniform teeth found in crocodilians with slender snouts.
facts.quote: Crocodilians with slender snouts generally possess needle-like caniniform teeth, whereas those in the mandible of Ultrastenos are molariforms

facts.statement: Yates and Stein identified a White Hunter cranium as likely belonging to the same individual as the holotype of Baru huberi, which shows mesorostral and platyrostral morphology.
facts.quote: Yates and Stein identified one of the White Hunter crania as having most likely been derived from the same individual as the holotype of "Baru" huberi, which consists of a partial rostrum clearly showing mesorostral and platyrostral morphology

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that the development of slender jaws in mekosuchines may have been prevented by developmental constraints similar to those in alligators.
facts.quote: it is possible that much like alligators, the development of slender jaws within this group is prevented by certain developmental constraints that occur during the growth of these animals

facts.statement: It is possible that piscivory was not a viable lifestyle for mekosuchines throughout much of Australia's prehistory.
facts.quote: Alternatively, it is possible that piscivory, unlike other lifestyles, was simply not viable throughout much of Australia's prehistory

facts.statement: Another hypothesis suggests that mekosuchines could not become longirostrine because other crocodilians already occupied that ecological niche.
facts.quote: Another possibility posits that mekosuchines were barred from becoming longirostrine due to the presence of other crocodilians already occupying this niche

facts.statement: Stein et al. (2016) classified Ultrastenos as a mekosuchine crocodilian and a sister taxon to Trilophosuchus rackhami.
facts.quote: In Stein et al. (2016) Ultrastenos is recovered as a mekosuchine crocodilian and sister taxa to Trilophosuchus rackhami

facts.statement: Rio and Mannion published a study in 2021 discussing the phylogenetic position of Ultrastenos.
facts.quote: Another study discussing the phylogenetic position of Ultrastenos was that of Rio and Mannion, published in 2021

facts.statement: Lee and Yates (2018) recovered "Baru" huberi as closely related to the Bullock Creek taxon.
facts.quote: Lee and Yates (2018), "Baru" huberi was recovered as being closely related to the Bullock Creek taxon

facts.statement: Ristevski et al. (2023) found a clade linking "Baru" huberi and dwarf mekosuchines, excluding Quinkana.
facts.quote: Ristevski et al. 2023 do much the same to the exclusion of Quinkana

facts.statement: The parent group of Ultrastenos is Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Mekosuchinae

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Ultrastenos is Ultrastenos willisi.
facts.quote: Type species: Ultrastenos willisi

facts.statement: Ultrastenos lived during the Chattian stage, from 27.3 to 23.04 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Chattian to Chattian (27.3 to 23.04 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ultrastenos fossils are known from two Oligocene localities in the Riversleigh World Heritage Area: the White Hunter Site and the Low Lion Site.
facts.quote: Ultrastenos is known from two Oligocene localities of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area, the White Hunter Site and the Low Lion Site

facts.statement: Ultrastenos is believed to have been a semi-aquatic generalist with a broad, platyrostral skull, similar to Baru wickeni.
facts.quote: Ultrastenos and Baru wickeni are thought to have been much more similar in niche. Both are believed to have been semi-aquatic generalists due to their broad, platyrostral skulls

facts.statement: During the Late Oligocene, the Low Lion Site was covered by open forests lacking extensive river systems or wetlands.
facts.quote: During the Late Oligocene the Low Lion Site was predominantly covered by open forests but lacks evidence for extensive river systems or wetlands from this region

facts.statement: Ultrastenos likely inhabited forest lakes and ponds drained by karstic limestone.
facts.quote: Instead, Ultrastenos may have been more at home in forest lakes and ponds that were drained through the underlying karstic limestone
